rules.ruleTitle: Subject and finite verb agree in person and number
rules.canonicalRule: A finite verb normally agrees with its grammatical subject in person and number; do not let nearby nouns override the true subject.
rules.commonTrap: Choosing a verb by the nearest visible noun rather than the grammatical subject.
rules.verificationNote: Verified against Cambridge Grammar subject–verb agreement guidance.

rules.ruleTitle: Ignore intervening prepositional/additive phrases when finding the subject
rules.canonicalRule: A prepositional or parenthetical phrase between subject and verb does not change the number of the head subject.
rules.commonTrap: The quality of these apples are... / The report with its annexures were...
rules.verificationNote: Verified from Cambridge head-subject agreement principles.

rules.ruleTitle: As well as does not create a compound subject
rules.canonicalRule: With X, as well as Y, the verb normally agrees with X, the grammatical head subject; the as-well-as phrase is additional information.
rules.commonTrap: The chief engineer, as well as two assistants, are expected...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against Cambridge Grammar; as well as is not equivalent to and for agreement.

rules.ruleTitle: Together with / along with do not change the head subject
rules.canonicalRule: Phrases such as together with and along with add accompanying information; the finite verb normally agrees with the head subject before the phrase.
rules.commonTrap: The manager, along with the assistants, were...
rules.verificationNote: Verified from Cambridge agreement and with-phrase principles; use unambiguous formal examples.

rules.ruleTitle: A number of + plural noun takes plural agreement
rules.canonicalRule: A number of + plural noun means several/many and takes plural agreement.
rules.commonTrap: A number of candidates has...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against Cambridge number expressions and plural agreement usage.

rules.ruleTitle: The number of + plural noun takes singular agreement
rules.canonicalRule: When the subject is the number of + plural noun, the head is singular number, so the verb is singular.
rules.commonTrap: The number of applications have increased...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against Cambridge number-expression usage; the grammatical head is number.

rules.ruleTitle: Each of + plural noun/pronoun is singular in formal agreement
rules.canonicalRule: Each is grammatically singular; in formal exam English, each of + plural noun/pronoun takes a singular finite verb.
rules.commonTrap: Each of the members have submitted...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against Cambridge Grammar.

rules.ruleTitle: Every + singular count noun takes singular agreement
rules.canonicalRule: Every is followed by a singular count noun and normally takes a singular verb.
rules.commonTrap: Every candidates are...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against Cambridge Grammar.

rules.ruleTitle: Many a + singular noun takes singular agreement
rules.canonicalRule: The formal construction many a + singular count noun normally takes a singular verb.
rules.commonTrap: Many a candidates have...
rules.verificationNote: Formal pattern cross-checked against standard dictionary/grammar usage; use unambiguous SSC-style contexts.

rules.ruleTitle: More than one + singular noun normally takes singular agreement
rules.canonicalRule: The expression more than one is normally followed by a singular noun and singular verb despite its plural meaning.
rules.commonTrap: More than one candidate have...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against standard dictionary usage; use only clear formal examples.

rules.ruleTitle: Either of + plural noun/pronoun takes singular agreement in formal exam English
rules.canonicalRule: Either as a pronoun referring to one of two is singular in formal agreement: either of the options is acceptable.
rules.commonTrap: Either of the plans are...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against formal either usage; conversational variation should not be used to create ambiguous items.

rules.ruleTitle: Neither of + plural noun/pronoun takes singular agreement in formal exam English
rules.canonicalRule: Neither as a pronoun meaning not either one is treated as singular in formal exam English: neither of the answers is correct.
rules.commonTrap: Neither of the answers are correct in a formal SSC item.
rules.verificationNote: Use formal singular agreement to avoid conversational variation.

rules.ruleTitle: Either...or with different-number subjects: agreement commonly follows the nearer subject
rules.canonicalRule: In formal exam items with either...or and subjects of different number, place the verb to agree naturally with the nearer subject; rewrite awkward combinations rather than forcing ambiguity.
rules.commonTrap: Either the assistants or the manager are responsible.
rules.verificationNote: Verified against standard proximity usage; item writer must avoid constructions where native usage varies.

rules.ruleTitle: Neither...nor with different-number subjects: agreement commonly follows the nearer subject
rules.canonicalRule: In formal exam items with neither...nor and subjects of different number, the verb is normally aligned with the nearer subject; prefer naturally ordered, unambiguous sentences.
rules.commonTrap: Neither the manager nor his assistants was willing...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against standard formal usage; keep examples unambiguous.

rules.ruleTitle: Collective nouns: singular for unit, plural possible for members in British English
rules.canonicalRule: Collective nouns such as committee/team can take singular agreement when viewed as one unit; British English can use plural agreement when emphasizing members acting individually.
rules.commonTrap: Treating every collective noun as obligatorily singular in all contexts.
rules.verificationNote: Critical ambiguity guard: only ask when context clearly signals unit vs members; never mark a legitimate BrE alternative wrong without context.

rules.ruleTitle: News is grammatically singular
rules.canonicalRule: News ends in -s but is an uncountable singular noun and takes singular agreement.
rules.commonTrap: The news are encouraging.
rules.verificationNote: Verified from Cambridge Dictionary countability and examples.

rules.ruleTitle: Academic subjects such as mathematics are singular when naming a field
rules.canonicalRule: Names of academic subjects ending in -s, such as mathematics, normally take singular agreement when referring to the field of study.
rules.commonTrap: Mathematics are difficult.
rules.verificationNote: Verified by dictionary grammar label and examples.

rules.ruleTitle: Plural-only nouns take plural agreement
rules.canonicalRule: Plural-only nouns such as scissors, trousers and premises (in relevant senses) take plural agreement unless used with a singular measure expression such as a pair of.
rules.commonTrap: The scissors is blunt.
rules.verificationNote: Verified against Cambridge plural-only noun guidance.

rules.ruleTitle: A pair of + plural-only noun has singular head pair
rules.canonicalRule: In a pair of scissors/trousers, the grammatical head pair is singular, so singular agreement is normal.
rules.commonTrap: A pair of scissors are on the desk.
rules.verificationNote: Verified via head-noun agreement principles.

rules.ruleTitle: Amount/distance/time expression can take singular agreement when viewed as one unit
rules.canonicalRule: A plural-looking measure of money, distance, time or quantity often takes a singular verb when the whole amount is treated as a single unit.
rules.commonTrap: Ten kilometres are a long way to walk in this context.
rules.verificationNote: Use contexts that clearly present the measure as one total quantity.

rules.ruleTitle: Fractions/percentages agree with the noun in the of-phrase
rules.canonicalRule: With fractions or percentages followed by of + noun, agreement normally follows whether the noun denotes singular/uncountable material or plural count entities.
rules.commonTrap: Fifty percent of the work are complete / fifty percent of the students is absent.
rules.verificationNote: Verified against percentage agreement principles.

rules.ruleTitle: One of + plural count noun
rules.canonicalRule: After one of, use a plural count noun: one of the candidates, one of the best solutions.
rules.commonTrap: One of the candidate.
rules.contrastWith: the only one of those who...
rules.verificationNote: Verified against standard one-of construction.

rules.ruleTitle: One of those + plural noun + who + plural verb
rules.canonicalRule: In the standard construction one of those + plural noun + who..., the relative pronoun refers to the plural antecedent, so the relative-clause verb is plural.
rules.commonTrap: She is one of those researchers who works late.
rules.contrastWith: the only one of those who + singular
rules.verificationNote: Verified from relative-pronoun antecedent principles; use only unambiguous 'one of those + plural + who' items.
